strengths: The paper addresses a genuine limitation of prior context compression methods (the reliance on an autoencoding objective that is misaligned with downstream tasks) and proposes a conceptually clean alternative that derives compressed representations directly from selected context tokens, which is intuitively appealing and training-efficient.

The empirical results are consistent: SAC outperforms strong baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, LLMLingua-2) across multiple compression ratios and on both in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA tasks, with the margin widening at higher compression ratios (15x, 51x), where improvements are non-trivial (e.g., 54.95 vs. 51.52 F1 at 15x ID).

The ablation studies are relatively thorough, isolating the contribution of the anchor embedding, bidirectional attention, the token-selection strategy, and the AE/LM objectives, and showing that SAC is robust to different token-selection strategies (Lingua-2 vs. uniform).

The analysis section, including attention-map visualization and t-SNE of key/value representations, provides a useful (if somewhat qualitative) explanation for why anchoring representations within the original context yields more compatible compressed KVs for the target LLM.
The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and includes a reproducibility statement with an anonymous code link and detailed hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method is essentially a combination of well-established ideas (token selection / importance-based selection as in LLMLingua and SelectiveContext, KV-based compression as in 500xCompressor, and bidirectional attention as in LLM2Vec/NV-Embed). The authors themselves acknowledge SAC 'can be seen as a combination of token selection methods and compressed token training methods,' and the default selection strategy is directly borrowed from EPL (middle token of each chunk), so the core architectural novelty is modest.

The improvements at the practically most relevant 5x compression ratio are very small (e.g., ID 63.63 vs. 62.90 F1, 46.95 vs. 46.33 EM; OOD 47.72 vs. 46.95 F1, 32.30 vs. 31.30 EM), and no statistical significance or variance across seeds is reported, making it unclear whether these gains are within noise. The large 'maximum improvement' figures quoted in the abstract/intro are relative comparisons against the weakest baseline (ICAE) and are somewhat misleading.

The central motivation of context compression is inference efficiency (latency and memory reduction), yet the paper never measures inference speed, memory savings, or FLOPs of the compressed model versus the full-context model. Only training time and LM perplexity are reported in the appendix, which does not substantiate the efficiency claims.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: a single, small backbone (Llama-3.2-1B) and only extractive QA tasks from MRQA. It is unclear whether the approach scales to larger models (e.g., 7B+) or generalizes to other long-context tasks such as summarization, multi-turn dialogue, or generation, despite the introduction motivating these use cases.

The claim that autoencoding is unnecessary is not conclusively established. The evidence rests largely on a single re-implementation of 500xCompressor that 'does not fully support' the earlier finding of ICAE, and SAC's own AE+LM variant performs comparably to LM-only in several settings (e.g., OOD 5x: 47.26 vs. 47.72 F1), so the argument that AE is inherently misaligned is weaker than presented.

The interpretation of the attention visualizations is debatable: a sparse, diagonal attention pattern for SAC is claimed to indicate better 'local focus,' but this could equally suggest that anchors fail to aggregate global context—the opposite of what compression requires. The representation analysis is qualitative and does not include quantitative metrics (e.g., reconstruction/retrieval alignment) to support the claimed KV-space compatibility.

Baseline fairness and tuning are not fully documented. It is unclear whether ICAE/500xCompressor/EPL were trained to convergence under their original best configurations or under a uniform setting that might disadvantage them, and LLMLingua-2 (hard compression) is compared under a different training regime, making cross-paradigm comparisons difficult to interpret.

The naming and framing of 'semantic anchors' overstate the method's semantic grounding, since anchors are selected by position (chunk midpoints) rather than by any semantic criterion; the semantic prior comes only from reusing original token embeddings.

strengths: Proposes a conceptually simple and intuitive approach to context compression by selecting anchor tokens directly from the context and using their KV representations, avoiding the autoencoding objective used in prior work.

Provides useful ablations on key components (bidirectional attention, anchor embeddings, token selection strategy) and on the effect of the autoencoding objective, offering some insight into why AE may be unnecessary when anchors are semantically meaningful.
Evaluates on multiple MRQA datasets (in-domain and out-of-domain) across several compression ratios, with some gains over strong baselines such as EPL, particularly at higher compression ratios.
The paper is generally clear and well-organized, with a straightforward method description and supplementary visualization analyses.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method combines token selection, KV-based compression, and bidirectional attention in a fairly incremental way. Similar ideas appear in prompt compression, embedding models, and prior compression work.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistent. At 5x compression, improvements over EPL are small (e.g., 0.77 F1 / 1.0 EM on OOD average), and SAC underperforms on several individual datasets (e.g., BioASQ, RACE, RE at 51x OOD). No statistical significance tests or error bars are provided.

Several important technical details are missing: how bidirectional attention is implemented for a causal LLM, how anchor token position IDs are handled when concatenating sub-contexts, how the target LLM consumes the compressed KV pairs, and how anchor embeddings are trained.

Evaluation is narrow: only question answering on MRQA with a single 1B model is considered. No other task types (summarization, dialogue, long-document reasoning) or model scales are tested. Despite acceleration being a primary motivation, no inference latency or memory measurements are reported.
Reproducibility is weakened by an apparently missing code link (the text says 'This code' without a URL) and insufficient implementation details for reproducing the core architecture.

Some claims are overstated: SAC still relies on language modeling pretraining and QA finetuning, so 'autoencoding-free' is accurate but the broader framing of 'eliminating the need for training' is not. Similarly, 'consistently outperforms' is not supported on a per-dataset basis.
The representation and attention analyses are qualitative and do not establish a causal link to downstream performance; the t-SNE plots lack quantitative metrics.
The paper does not compare against other relevant compression methods (e.g., GIST, AutoCompressor, xRAG) or discuss in depth why they are excluded beyond target LLM finetuning concerns.

strengths: Proposes SAC, an autoencoding-free context compression method that selects anchor tokens directly from the original context and aggregates information into their KV representations, avoiding the reconstruction mismatch of autoencoding objectives.

Clear and intuitive motivation: autoencoding forces compression tokens to reconstruct all tokens, including low-information ones, which diverges from downstream tasks; SAC leverages the semantic priors of original context tokens instead.

Empirical results on MRQA in-domain and out-of-domain across 5x, 15x, and 51x compression ratios show consistent improvements over strong baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, LLMLingua-2), with larger gains at higher compression ratios.

Comprehensive ablations validate key components: bidirectional attention and anchor embeddings both contribute, token selection is robust (Lingua-2-based selection also works), and removing the autoencoding objective often improves performance.
Analysis via attention maps and t-SNE visualizations provides useful insight into why SAC works, e.g., anchor representations remain closer to original context KVs and attend more locally.

Good reproducibility support: code, hyperparameters, training details, and detailed per-dataset results are provided in the appendix; SAC also trains about 31% faster than ICAE due to avoiding the AE task.
Well-written and clearly positioned relative to prior work, making the contribution easy to understand.
weaknesses: Evaluation scope is narrow: only MRQA (extractive QA) and a single 1B model (Llama-3.2-1B). No other downstream tasks (e.g., summarization, generation, long-context reasoning) or larger models are tested, limiting claims of broad generalization.
Performance gains at 5x compression are modest (e.g., in-domain avg F1 63.63 vs. EPL 62.90; out-of-domain avg F1 47.72 vs. 46.95), with the main advantage emerging only at higher compression ratios.

Several implementation details are missing or unclear: how compressed KV pairs are integrated into the target LLM, what position IDs are used for anchor tokens, the exact bidirectional attention mask, and how sub-context boundaries are handled. This may hinder reproducibility.
Novelty is moderate: SAC combines existing ideas (token selection, LoRA, bidirectional attention, KV compression) and removes AE; the core technical components are not entirely new.
No statistical significance tests or multiple runs are reported, so it is unclear how sensitive the results are to random seeds or hyperparameters.
The default anchor selection strategy (middle token of each chunk) is a simple heuristic; chunk size and alternative selection granularities are not explored.
Some claims are slightly stronger than the evidence: 'significantly outperforms' is not always supported at 5x compression, and 'autoencoding-free' still requires LM pretraining and QA finetuning.
The AE ablation shows only small differences at 5x compression, so the necessity of removing AE is not fully compelling across all compression ratios.

strengths: Proposes SAC, an autoencoding-free context compression method that selects anchor tokens directly from the context and compresses information into their KV representations, avoiding the need for autoencoding pretraining.
Introduces two effective components: anchor embeddings to mark selected tokens and bidirectional attention to allow anchors to aggregate information from the full context.
Comprehensive experiments on MRQA (in-domain and out-of-domain) and long-context summarization, across multiple compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x) and model sizes (1B, 3B, 8B).
Consistently outperforms strong baselines such as ICAE, 500xCompressor, EPL, DAST, Activation Beacon, and LLMLingua-2 on QA tasks.
Ablation studies validate the contributions of anchor embeddings and bidirectional attention, and analyze different token selection strategies.
Efficiency analysis (FLOPs and empirical latency) shows SAC is more efficient than 500xCompressor despite using bidirectional attention.
Attention visualization and t-SNE representation analysis provide qualitative insights into why SAC's compressed representations are better aligned with the original context.
Reproducibility statement and claimed release of code, model, and data (though the link is missing in the manuscript).
weaknesses: Missing critical implementation details on how positional information is handled for compressed anchor tokens, especially when concatenating sub-contexts and feeding them to the decoder. EPL explicitly addresses position IDs, but SAC does not explain this, which raises soundness and reproducibility concerns.

The gradient cosine similarity analysis is technically flawed: orthogonal gradients (cosine similarity near zero) do not imply interference; interference would be indicated by negative similarity. The claim that orthogonality causes optimization conflict is incorrect.
Uses ROUGE-1 F1 as the primary metric for QA, which is non-standard (typically token-level F1 and EM are used). Although EM is also reported, this choice may hinder direct comparison with prior work.

Long-context summarization evaluation is limited: only EPL is used as a baseline, only ROUGE-1 F1 is reported, and the gain on QMSum is negligible (14.95 vs 14.82). The claim of consistent superiority on summarization is overstated.
The autoencoding-free claim is validated mainly for SAC; for 500xCompressor, AE+LM generally helps. The broader conclusion that autoencoding may not be essential is not fully supported.
The code/model/data link is missing in the manuscript's reproducibility statement and abstract, making it difficult to verify the claimed release.
The reference list contains obvious formatting errors and repeated nonsense text, indicating a lack of careful proofreading.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines existing ideas (token selection, anchor embeddings, bidirectional attention) and the improvement over the strongest baseline EPL is modest at 5x compression (e.g., +0.73 F1 on in-domain average).
No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported; results may be sensitive to random seeds.
Overclaims in the abstract and conclusion that SAC consistently outperforms existing context compression methods on summarization, while only EPL is compared and the gains are small.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel context compression architecture, SAC, that avoids autoencoding pretraining by selecting anchor tokens from the original context and aggregating information into their KV representations. This is a conceptually interesting direction that shifts from learned compression tokens to using semantically meaningful anchors.

The proposed bidirectional attention modification for anchor tokens is a reasonable architectural choice to enable them to access the full context, and the ablation studies demonstrate its importance.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, covering multiple QA datasets (in-domain and out-of-domain), different compression ratios (5x, 15x, 51x), model sizes (1B, 3B, 8B), and long-context summarization tasks.

The paper provides detailed analysis including attention visualization, representation analysis (t-SNE), and gradient cosine similarity to support the claim that autoencoding objectives can conflict with downstream tasks.

The method shows consistent improvements over strong baselines (ICAE, 500xCompressor, Activation Beacon, DAST, EPL) across most settings, with particularly notable gains at higher compression ratios and larger model sizes.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental: the core idea of selecting anchor tokens from the context and using their KV representations is essentially a combination of token selection (e.g., LLMLingua-2) and soft compression (e.g., EPL). The paper acknowledges that SAC builds upon EPL's position layout, and the main architectural change is adding an anchor embedding and bidirectional attention. The improvement over EPL is modest (e.g., 1-3 points F1 on average), which may not be sufficient to justify a top-tier conference acceptance.

The central claim that autoencoding tasks conflict with downstream tasks is not rigorously established. The gradient cosine similarity analysis (Figure 9) shows orthogonality but does not prove that AE causes performance degradation; it could be that AE simply adds noise. The ablation in Table 5 shows SAC(w/ AE+LM) is close to SAC, and for 500x, AE+LM sometimes outperforms LM-only, contradicting the claimed misalignment. The paper's own results are mixed.

The efficiency advantage is not fully evaluated. The paper compares FLOPs and compression time against 500xCompressor, but the more relevant comparison is against the target LLM without compression. Since SAC still processes the full context during compression (with bidirectional attention over all tokens), the overall inference cost (compression + generation) may not be lower than a full-context baseline for moderate compression ratios. The paper lacks an end-to-end latency comparison.

The token selection strategy is simplistic (uniform middle token of each chunk). The paper shows random selection is worse, but does not compare against more sophisticated selection methods like attention-based or perplexity-based selection. The Lingua-2-based selection performs similarly to uniform, suggesting the selection strategy may not be critical, but this is not thoroughly explored.

The paper claims SAC is 'autoencoding-free', but it still requires a pretraining stage with the LM objective (20k steps). The distinction from prior work is that AE is omitted, but LM pretraining is still needed. The term 'autoencoding-free' is somewhat misleading; it's more accurate to say 'without AE objective' rather than 'without pretraining'.

The evaluation on long-context summarization shows very small gains over EPL (e.g., 14.95 vs 14.82 on QMSum), which is within noise. The paper does not report statistical significance or multiple runs, making it hard to assess the reliability of the improvements.

The paper does not compare against a strong token selection baseline (e.g., LLMLingua-2) trained with the same protocol. LLMLingua-2 is evaluated with a 5x compression ratio but performs poorly, which may be due to lack of fine-tuning on the target LLM. A fair comparison would require training a token selection method on the same data and model, which is missing.

The analysis of why SAC works (e.g., attention patterns, representation alignment) is qualitative and post-hoc. The claim that SAC's compressed representations 'more closely resemble original context token KVs' is supported by t-SNE visualizations, but no quantitative metric (e.g., CKA similarity) is provided to substantiate this.

The paper is written in a somewhat verbose and repetitive style, with many details relegated to the appendix. The main text lacks a clear, concise statement of the key insights and limitations. For example, the 'AE-LM Gradient Perspective' is only briefly mentioned and not fully developed.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: deriving compressed representations directly from selected context tokens (semantic anchors) rather than learning special compression tokens from scratch, thereby leveraging the semantic priors already present in the input. This is an intuitive and practically appealing design.

The paper provides a thorough and consistently favorable empirical evaluation: three compression ratios (5x/15x/51x), three model scales (1B/3B/8B), in-domain and out-of-domain MRQA tasks, two long-context summarization datasets, and a long-context QA benchmark. SAC beats strong baselines (EPL, 500xCompressor, DAST, Activation Beacon, ICAE) across essentially all settings.

The ablation studies are useful: they isolate the contributions of the anchor embedding and bidirectional attention, compare token selection strategies (random / Lingua-2 / uniform), and, importantly, directly test the AE-free hypothesis by training variants with/without AE and LM objectives.

The analysis section goes beyond numbers, using gradient cosine similarity to argue AE and LM gradients become orthogonal, t-SNE visualizations to show anchor KV representations remain close to context KV distributions, and attention maps to contrast SAC's focused pattern with more diffuse baselines.

Efficiency is addressed directly: a FLOPs analysis and an empirical latency comparison show SAC is actually cheaper than 500xCompressor despite bidirectional attention, since it avoids appending extra special tokens. Pretraining is also ~26-31% faster than baselines.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and accompanied by detailed appendices, hyperparameters, and a reproducibility statement with code/data release.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and largely combinatorial. Anchor-style token selection is related to prior token-selection methods, bidirectional/global attention is a known technique (LLM2Vec, NV-Embed), and the KV-as-representation follows 500xCompressor. The specific combination is reasonable but incremental, and the paper itself acknowledges SAC 'can be seen as building upon EPL' with representation enhancement.

The AE-is-harmful claim is somewhat overstated relative to the evidence. Table 5 shows mixed results (500x with AE+LM beats LM-only at 5x but not at 15x/51x), and the authors admit ICAE's findings do not generalize. Gradient orthogonality (Fig. 9) is suggestive but not causal. The conclusion that AE is 'not entirely essential' would benefit from a sharper mechanism or broader validation.

Baseline fairness is a concern. The paper claims all soft-compression baselines were trained under 'the same' settings/data, but Activation Beacon and DAST fall dramatically below their typical reported behavior (e.g., Beacon EM of 15.39/13.02), which suggests they may be under-tuned or ill-suited to this training regime. LLMLingua-2's very low scores on SQuAD (32.93 F1 at 5x) also warrant scrutiny, since the hard-compression comparison is coupled to the Full-FT model.

No variance or error bars are reported. Several headline gains are modest (e.g., 5x ID: SAC 63.63 vs EPL 62.90; OOD 47.72 vs 46.95), and without multiple seeds or significance testing it is unclear whether these differences are meaningful. The much larger gains shown in the abstract (up to 23-27%) are attributed to weaker baselines like ICAE.

Several methods details are under-specified: how position IDs are assigned to anchor tokens (relative to the EPL position layout discussion), whether/how the decoder distinguishes the compressed anchor KV from ordinary context KV, and precisely which KV layers are retained. The bidirectional-attention ablation removes the mask for all tokens, so the effect of bidirectional attention on anchors alone is not disentangled from removing causality globally.

Absolute performance remains far from the Full-FT model (e.g., ~55 vs ~71 F1 at 15x), and the practical deployment value of a compression scheme with such a large gap is not discussed. The practical significance of the AE-free bonus is somewhat undercut by the fact that all methods still require 40k training steps and the reported gain in absolute terms is a modest improvement over EPL.
